item.title: - What binds the world? What leads the world? By abandoning what thing Is Nibbāna called? - Delight binds the world, Seeking leads the world,…
item.description:
- What binds the world?
What leads the world?
By abandoning what thing
Is Nibbāna called?
- Delight binds the world,
Seeking leads the world,
By abandoning craving,
Is Nibbāna called.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.64
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - What hangs up the world? What envelops the world? What closes in the world? Upon what does the world stand? - Craving hangs up…
item.description:
- What hangs up the world?
What envelops the world?
What closes in the world?
Upon what does the world stand?
- Craving hangs up the world,
Aging envelops the world,
Death closes in the world,
Upon suffering the world stands.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.67
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, through lust, one is not freed. Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form…
item.description:
“Monks, through lust, one is not freed. Through lust for form, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With form as its object, with form as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Through lust for feeling … for perception … for formations, monks, consciousness becomes established with a foothold. With formations as its object, with formations as its support, seeking delight, it grows, increases, and expands. Monks, if anyone says: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will show the coming and going, the passing away and arising, the growth, increase, and expansion of consciousness’ — such a thing is not possible. Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the form element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. If a monk has abandoned lust for the feeling element … for the perception element … for the formation element … Monks, if a monk has abandoned lust for the consciousness element — with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, the support of consciousness does not exist. Without that support, consciousness does not expand, does not generate activity, and is liberated. Being liberated, it is steady; being steady, it is content; being content, it is not agitated; being not agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.53
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached…
item.description:
“Monks, if there were no gratification in form, beings would not become attached to form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become attached to form. If there were no peril in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because there is peril in form, beings become disenchanted with form. And, monks, as long as beings do not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, and the escape as escape in regard to these five aggregates of clinging, they have not, monks, escaped from this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans; they are not free from it, not detached, not liberated, their minds are not at ease. But when they directly know these five aggregates … as they actually are, then they have escaped … their minds are at ease.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.28
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing.…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds cognizable by the ear … Odors cognizable by the nose … Tastes cognizable by the tongue … Tangibles cognizable by the body—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has…
item.description:
“Monks, form is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past form, does not delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form. Feeling is impermanent … Perception is impermanent … Formations are impermanent … Consciousness is impermanent, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.9
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Householder, suppose a person borrows goods — luxurious vehicles, fine jewelry and ornaments — and with those borrowed goods he goes through the market, being…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose a person borrows goods — luxurious vehicles, fine jewelry and ornaments — and with those borrowed goods he goes through the market, being honored and surrounded by many people. The crowd sees him and says: ‘This person is truly wealthy, and the wealthy enjoy such things.’ But wherever the owners see him, they take back their possessions. What do you think, householder? Is that person’s disguise then ended?” “Yes, venerable sir. Why is that? Because the owners take back their possessions.” … “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander…
item.description:
“Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander for the happiness of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, happiness, and welfare of gods and humans. Do not go two by the same road. Monks, teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing. Proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, if they do not hear the Dhamma, will decline. They will become those who understand the Dhamma. Monks, I will go to Uruvelā, the town of Senā, to teach the Dhamma.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.5
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks,…
item.description:
“Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks, the five hindrances subsist in dependence on food, with food as condition they stand; without food they do not stand. And what, monks, is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire? There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful. Frequent unwise attention to it — this is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “All conditioned things are impermanent” — When one sees this with wisdom, One becomes disenchanted with suffering — This is the path to purity. “All…
item.description:
“All conditioned things are impermanent” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

“All conditioned things are suffering” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

“All phenomena are not-self” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

From: Dhammapada 273-289
📖 Read this sutta
